answer.observations: Baseline r001 with defaults: udp_goodput_bps=979021120, udp_loss_frac=0.510489, tcp_goodput_bps=0, tcp_retrans=3, l1_util=0.999999, l1_drops=911591.

findings.text: tcp_goodput_bps=0 while UDP saturates l1 (l1_util=0.999999) and TCP retransmits only 3 segments.
findings.name: TCP starved by UDP

whys.result: With defaults, tcp_goodput_bps=0 while udp_goodput_bps=979021120 and l1_drops=911591.
whys.guess: The 2Gbps UDP flow keeps the sender-side FIFO queue full, so TCP packets are dropped before TCP can deliver payload.

whys.result: The default tcp_goodput_bps=0 occurs with l1.queue.length=100.
whys.guess: The 100-packet FIFO queue length is the proximate cause: a much shorter queue would reduce persistent fullness and allow some TCP packets through.

whys.result: The default tcp_goodput_bps=0 occurs with TcpCubic and tcp_retrans=3.
whys.guess: TcpCubic's loss-based response to UDP-induced drops makes TCP back off, while TcpBbr could maintain inflight and obtain bandwidth.

whys.result: The default tcp_goodput_bps=0 occurs with a FIFO queue on l1.
whys.guess: FIFO scheduling lets UDP monopolize the link; a scheduler queue that gives each flow an equal link share would raise tcp_goodput_bps.

hypotheses.text: Reducing l1.queue.length from 100 to 4 while keeping TcpCubic increases tcp_goodput_bps above the default value.
Changing tcp.type from TcpCubic to TcpBbr while keeping l1.queue.length=100 increases tcp_goodput_bps above the default value.
Replacing the sender-side FIFO queue on l1 with a scheduler queue while keeping default settings increases tcp_goodput_bps above the default value.

answer.observations: E1: q4 and bbr still have tcp_goodput_bps=0, while scheduler r004 has tcp_goodput_bps=482007923. V3: the scheduler test was inconclusive because scheduler scheduling and queue-length effects were not separated.

whys.result: With scheduler queue r004 tcp_goodput_bps=482007923 while FIFO r001 is 0.
whys.guess: Per-flow scheduling gives TCP a service share, so TCP goodput is set by that share and packet overhead rather than by FIFO queue length or TCP variant.

whys.result: The scheduler run r004 has tcp_goodput_bps=482007923 with default queue length 100.
whys.guess: The scheduler result is caused by its 100-packet per-flow buffering; with l1.queue.length=4 the scheduler would starve TCP like FIFO.

hypotheses.text: At the same l1.queue.length (4 and 100) and TcpCubic, a sender-side scheduler queue gives higher tcp_goodput_bps than a FIFO queue.

answer.observations: E1 shows scheduler r004 has tcp_goodput_bps=482007923 while FIFO r001/r002 have 0; V3 says the scheduler test was not fair because queue-length and scheduling effects were not separated. F2 needs an explanation for r004 reverse utilization 0.009208 with no reverse drops.

whys.result: r004 has tcp_goodput_bps=482007923, l1_util_back=0.009208, and l1_drops_back=0, while r001 has tcp_goodput_bps=0 and l1_util_back=0.0.
whys.guess: The reverse utilization is TCP ACK traffic from the scheduler-given TCP flow; ACK volume is low enough that the receiver-side queue drops none.

whys.result: r001 has tcp_goodput_bps=0, tcp_retrans=3, l1_drops=911591, and l1_util=0.999999.
whys.guess: TCP is stalled in persistent RTO: FIFO tail drops its initial/probe segments, cwnd stays minimal, and exponential RTO limits it to a few retransmissions.

hypotheses.text: At l1.queue.length=100 and TcpCubic, a sender-side scheduler queue gives higher mean tcp_bps than a FIFO queue.
At l1.queue.length=4 and TcpCubic, a sender-side scheduler queue gives higher mean tcp_bps than a FIFO queue.

drop.why: It combined queue lengths 4 and 100 in one claim; split into H5 and H6 so each rule compares simulations differing only in queue discipline.

answer.observations: V4/C4: scheduler at length 4 gives tcp_bps_mean=463881280 vs FIFO 0. T3-T8: r001 max tcp_inflight=1448, max tcp_rto_ms=8000, max tcp_cwnd=14480, max l1_devq_back=0; r004 max l1_devq_back=0.

whys.result: r001 max tcp_inflight=1448, max tcp_rto_ms=8000, max tcp_cwnd=14480, max l1_wait_ms=1.144.
whys.guess: FIFO TCP is RTO-stalled: cwnd can open but only one segment stays unacked, so exponential RTO dominates and payload delivery is zero.

whys.result: scheduler r004 tcp_goodput=482007923 and r005 tcp_bps_mean=463881280, both near half of 1Gbps after overhead.
whys.guess: Scheduler gives TCP an equal service share; goodput is set by that share and packet overhead, not by TCP variant or larger queue.

whys.result: r004/r001 max l1_devq_back=0; r004 l1_util_back=0.009208 with tcp_goodput=482007923, r001 l1_util_back=0 with tcp_goodput=0.
whys.guess: Reverse utilization is TCP ACK traffic, low enough that the receiver-side queue never fills.

whys.result: FIFO TcpBbr r003 has tcp_goodput=0, while scheduler TcpCubic r004/r005 have nonzero TCP goodput.
whys.guess: Under scheduler, TcpBbr's bandwidth probing could let TCP exceed the equal-share payload rate, so tcp.type matters.

whys.result: scheduler length4 r005 has tcp_retrans=3417 and tcp_goodput=463881280, while length100 r004 has tcp_retrans=71 and tcp_goodput=482007923.
whys.guess: A larger scheduler queue would reduce TCP drops further and could raise tcp_goodput_bps above the length-100 value.

hypotheses.text: With a sender-side scheduler at l1.queue.length=100, TcpBbr's tcp_goodput_bps differs from TcpCubic's by at most 1%.
With a sender-side scheduler and TcpCubic, l1.queue.length=1000 gives tcp_goodput_bps no more than 1% above l1.queue.length=100.

drop.why: The existing scheduler-versus-FIFO comparison at length 100 was not certified fair, and H6 already tests the scheduler discipline at length 4.

answer.observations: E1/E2 show scheduler gives TCP about 482 Mbps at length 100 and 464 Mbps at length 4, while FIFO gives 0. T3-T12 show r001 TCP inflight stuck at 1448 bytes and RTO up to 8000 ms; T7/T8/T13/T14 show reverse device queue never fills.
